source.title: TinyLLM: A Framework for Training and Deploying Language Models at the Edge Computers
source.authors: Savitha Viswanadh Kandala; Pramuka Medaranga; Ambuj Varshney

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream accuracy across model sizes, a different measure from the claim’s held-out pretraining loss and compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream sensor-task accuracy for fine-tuned models at several parameter counts. It does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy across sizes, fits of power laws, extrapolation from small runs, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. The accuracy results in Figure 10 compare different model families and sizes; the authors summarize that larger models do not always achieve high accuracy and smaller custom models can be comparable or better. The reported training-token and training-compute figures are not loss-scaling results.
record.test_reason: Figure 12 sweeps five GPT-2-style custom models (30M–124M), pretrained on the same mix, and reports fine-tuned accuracy on three sensor tasks. This bears weakly on V6 in a new setting. No pretraining loss, power-law fits or allocation results are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: small custom-pretrained, fine-tuned models (30M–124M) can match or beat much larger off-the-shelf models on the sensor tasks, and domain-specific pretraining data improves them.
record.recipe_differences: Measures fine-tuned downstream sensor-task accuracy across a small model-size sweep, rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy or loss scaling against parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Accuracy varies with task dataset and model size; the paper reports poor results for the smallest models on gesture and minor exceptions to the overall size trend.
record.problems: The claim-relevant downstream results are limited to three sensor datasets and custom models from 30M to 124M parameters. Figure 12 values are not stated in the text, preventing exact point-by-point comparison. The paper reports accuracy after fine-tuning, not held-out pretraining loss; the Figure 10 comparison also mixes model families and training histories.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No compute-optimal allocation sweep; all sizes are trained on the same ~10B tokens.
Depth and width are varied together (C=64l); there is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
No loss power law under fine-tuning or for sensor data.
No functional fit, no prediction from pretraining loss, and no test of predictability. The sweep covers only five sizes within less than one order of magnitude.
No exponents or fitting choices are compared.

record.verdict_notes: This is a framework/systems paper; its scaling evidence is a small, figure-only size sweep (less than one order of magnitude) on downstream accuracy. The unspecified 'minor exceptions' and the abrupt 0% at 30M on gesture hint at non-smooth behaviour, but the text gives too little to label limits_scope. The Figure 11 data-mix experiment varies pretraining data composition, not scale, so it bears on no version.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss scaling against parameters, tokens, or compute is reported.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or optimal parameter/token scaling is reported.
The study does not isolate architecture effects at fixed parameter count; its smaller custom models change depth and hidden size together.
Fine-tuning is used, but the paper does not test whether power-law loss scaling holds in fine-tuning or other modalities and regimes.
Tests accuracy on a small set of fine-tuned sensor tasks and custom model sizes; does not test general downstream tasks or prediction from pretraining loss.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal split are fitted or compared across fitting choices.

rows.subject: Custom models (size-sweep aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Authors summarize accuracy across custom model sizes.
rows.value: Accuracy generally improves as parameter count increases, with minor exceptions.
rows.note: The text also says the 30M and 50M models perform poorly on gesture, and the 30M model has zero accuracy there.
rows.check: Authors state accuracy 'generally improves' with parameter count, with only 'minor exceptions'. That is near-full in direction, so observed rather than partial. Predictability (any fit or forecast) is not tested.

rows.subject: Fine-tuned off-the-shelf and custom models (comparison aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Model sizes shown in Figure 10; parameter counts not stated for each model
rows.operation_detail: Compared accuracy of fine-tuned models of different sizes.
rows.value: Authors state that larger models do not always have high accuracy and smaller custom models can be comparable to or better than larger models.
rows.note: Aggregate textual comparison across model families, rather than a controlled size sweep within one model family.
rows.check: Size here is file size in GB across different families (Phi, Llama, custom), quantization levels and pretraining data. The comparison is confounded and cannot isolate a scale effect.

relationships.condition: GPT-2-style custom models 30M–124M, same pretraining mix, LoRA fine-tuned on gesture, localisation and swimming tasks
relationships.reason: Authors report accuracy generally rises with parameter count, and the 30M model scores 0% on gesture (r16, r1). This is directional only, not a tested predictable law.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy generally increases with model size from 30M to 124M, while the 30M model achieves 0% gesture accuracy.
